The problem is that the very small values in the matrix are ignored by HiGHS. 

I've reproduced this (in C++) and get the following

> WARNING: LP matrix packed vector contains 20 |values| in [3.73378e-10, 3.73378e-10] less than or equal to 1e-09: ignored

and then, after solving, I get

> norm residual x on input equation is 0.0211851
norm residual x given by linprog is 0

If I set the `small_matrix_value` option to `1e-12`, as follows

> highs.setOptionValue("small_matrix_value", 1e-12);

then, after solving, I get

> norm residual x on input equation is 1.27628e-09
norm residual x given by linprog is 0

Conclusion: this is a very badly scaled model, and HiGHS has to protect itself against trying to solve models where such small matrix values are meaningful, as they can lead to numerical failure of the LP solvers. That said, in this case, the LP is so easy to solve - it's reduced to empty in presolve - that the small values aren't a problem.

The issue is that they aren't really warnings raised from `highspy` which can be handled within Python, but, AFAIK written out to the logging object, which is silenced from the Python bindings typically. e.g.:

```C++
  if (matrix_start[0]) {
    highsLogUser(log_options, HighsLogType::kWarning,
                 "%s matrix start vector begins with %" HIGHSINT_FORMAT
                 " rather than 0\n",
                 matrix_name.c_str(), matrix_start[0]);
    return HighsStatus::kError;
  }
```

This is also generally the default within `highspy` too:

```python
class Highs(_Highs):
...
    # Silence logging
    def silent(self, turn_off_output: bool = True):
        """
        Disables solver output to the console.
        """
        super().setOptionValue("output_flag", not turn_off_output)

# call_highs_from_python
h.setOptionValue("output_flag", False)
# also in test_highspy
# etc.
```

Will take a quick look into seeing if this is easily fixed within our wrappers, but seems a bit unlikely.

The occurrence of a warning like this results in a status return from passModel of kWarning, so it is available in code, not just from logging. 

Surely SciPy tests all status return values from highspy and takes appropriate action

>The occurrence of a warning like this results in a status return from passModel of kWarning, so it is available in code, not just from logging.
>

It does check the value, but...

```python
    init_status = highs.passModel(lp)
    if init_status == _h.HighsStatus.kError:
        # code to handle error here
    # continues normally
```

... only to check if there is an error. If there's a warning, it doesn't do anything.

If I add a line to print out the value of `init_status`, I get the following for the reprex in this case:

```
HighsStatus.kWarning
```

So HiGHS is returning that there is a warning.

Armed with this, I could write a piece of code which checks if there's a warning, then tells the user to turn on detailed logging.

```python
    init_status = highs.passModel(lp)
    if init_status == _h.HighsStatus.kError:
        # existing error handling code
    elif init_status == _h.HighsStatus.kWarning:
        warn(
            "A warning was encountered while passing the model. "
            "Set options={'disp': True'} to see it.",
            OptimizeWarning,
            stacklevel=3,
        )
```

Ideally, though, we would cut out the middle-man, and just tell the user what the warning was. I was looking through the source code of [highsLogUser()](https://github.com/ERGO-Code/HiGHS/blob/fd8665394edfd096c4f847c4a6fbc187364ef474/src/io/HighsIO.cpp#L96), and I realized that it accepts a callback to customize how logs are handled. We could set up a callback that records every warning that was seen while passing, presolving, or running the model.

You can use this from Python, too. You just need to set up a callback like this:

```python
highs = _h._Highs()
highs.setCallback(some_callable, None)
highs.startCallback(_h.cb.HighsCallbackType.kCallbackLogging)
```

I wrote a branch that uses this approach to turn HiGHS warnings into Python warnings. For the reprex in this issue, it prints the following:

```
/home/nodell/scipy/../foo/bug-20336.py:22: OptimizeWarning: LP matrix packed vector contains 20 |values| in [3.73378e-10, 3.73378e-10] less than or equal to 1e-09: ignored

  result = scipy.optimize.linprog(c, A_ub=None, b_ub=None, A_eq=a_eq, b_eq=b_eq, bounds=boundaries, options=dict(disp=False))
```

The branch can be found here: https://github.com/scipy/scipy/compare/main...nickodell:scipy:njo-log-warnings?expand=1

What do you think of this approach? There might be a performance hit, since it calls this callback every time there is a log message of any severity, not just warnings.

The reason this is silent for ND but not 1D is that the `_axis_nan_policy` decorator handles the ND case. For ND, the behavior with empty input is silent and correct (shape, dtype, and value if applicable) for every function the decorator is applied to, which is almost every reducing function in `stats` at this point. The behavior is tested exhaustively for 2D and 3D arrays with all valid `axis` arguments:
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/7f0a5cbc3854ffac20e75a4c36ea3575f051f393/scipy/stats/tests/test_axis_nan_policy.py#L690
(Probably unnecessary to keep doing this exhaustively, but at least I made the slowest parts XSLOW recently.)

For better or for worse, we made the decision in 2021 to the let the functions themselves handle the 1D case to preserve the old behavior, whatever it was. Every function had its own idea of what the right thing to do was when the input was empty _or too small_. Some were errors, and we didn't think that removing them and just returning NaNs (when NaN is the appropriate result) would be OK. For instance:
```python3
stats.skew([])
# nan with lots of warnings
stats.skewtest([])
# ValueError: skewtest is not valid with less than 8 samples; 0 samples were given.
```
It's not great that the behavior is different depending on the dimensionality, but we didn't think the new `axis` and `nan_policy` behavior should be as noisy and inconsistent as the old 1D behavior, yet we thought we needed to preserve the behavior for 1D input. We figured we'd pull the trigger and change the 1D case in SciPy 2.0. But based on the discussion in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/20496#discussion_r1572401090, maybe it would be OK to change it now?

It would be about as easy as uncommenting the code in this block:
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/7f0a5cbc3854ffac20e75a4c36ea3575f051f393/scipy/stats/_axis_nan_policy.py#L534-L538
Note that `NaN` is of the correct NumPy data type given the input, too. Functions (like `sum`) for which `nan` is not considered the correct result still get to return their own result.

Can we do this, and maybe emit a single, consistent warning for all reducing functions when the input is too small (in at least one slice)? (The warning can easily include the number of observations that is considered too small, if desired.)

I think that's the bit of tension here, right? The 1-D behavior with raising errors is quite reasonable (probably even preferred), but it becomes a problem specifically for `'omit'` and even more so in an n-D case where only one slice becomes too small?

Yes, exactly. We didn't think it made sense for a single short slice to cause the whole operation to error out.

> The 1-D behavior with raising errors is quite reasonable (probably even preferred)

In some contexts, yes. Then again, there's also an argument to be made for consistency within SciPy and between SciPy and NumPy. `np.mean` and `np.var` could have errored out, but for better or for worse, they set an example of returning `nan` with empty input. That's an appropriate result (if one is going to be returned) because the statistic is undefined. Many important SciPy functions (the moment functions, the t-tests, wilcoxon) followed suit. So it would make some sense for the rest to do the same, even in the 1D case, rather than the user having to guess.

Cases in which there are enough obvservations to calculate a numerical value of a statistic but not enough for the traditional, asymptotic p-value approximation to be accurate are bit more gray. At this point, it's very easy and quite fast to do so (e.g. see `method` of [`pearsonr`](https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/reference/generated/scipy.stats.pearsonr.html)).

The main difference between numpy and scipy are how things are prepared for the underlying LAPACK routine and which routine is used. NumPy makes very little preparation as it is already holding the object structure in it C codebase. SciPy on the other hand does a lot of hand-holding is it empty/is it 1d/is it properly dtyped and so on. That causes already some overhead which is quite expensive for small arrays. 

Then the actual time consumption happens due to the following difference. 

Scipy case 

```

   for each slice in ndarray:
    ---- This loop is in Python and slow / can't really be threaded
    ---- GIL is held here
       use f2py to prepare the slice suitable for LAPACK
            Change the dtype to one of np.float(32,64)/np.complex(64,128)
            Copy it to a Fortran ordered temporary array
            Make the call to LAPACK  <-- This LAPACK library might be threaded
    ----
```
So in summary SciPy treats each slice, almost*, a separate problem and loops everything in a Python loop.


In NumPy case is that slow loop is also in C and there is no theoretical blocker to loop in different threads, it can or won't thread it depending all the settings. 

Lately we have been moving this loop into C in SciPy too. We don't specifically release GIL there but we can. However it is just a faster loop and that's pretty much it. It is not calling LAPACK for different slices in different threads since the C code is not threaded. That's a nontrivial balance to strike depending on many architecture and OS details to get it right. The called LAPACK routine can be and most of the time is threaded, for example in OpenBLAS `?getrf` that `linalg.solve` uses runs parallel for sizes > 100. 

Long story short, it is a bit apples/oranges comparison. We will eventually get there but it is nontrivial work and any help is appreciated.

I agree with this. But wouldn't want to certify methods as being rock solid with other precisions. #22865 is only scratching the surface.

1. `approx_derivative` was not faithfully outputting np.float32 for fp32 `x0``/`fun(x0)`.
2. `ScalarFunction` was not producing 32 bit output for `fun` or `grad` when `x0` is a length one, fp32 array.
3. There was no consensus about what represented a fp32 problem. Is it a fp32 `x0` or `fun`?
4. No centralised way of setting linesearch parameters for different precisions for all the methods. It's unclear as to whether there are other gotchas that we don't know about along these lines. One can't focus on just one method to start with. One can't focus on just one method to start with.
5. Some methods with native code aren't usable (e.g. TNC/SLSQP) because of the typed nature of the inputs.
6. At least from my viewpoint of the knowledge of the code base, the maintainer group has historically thought of usage as being fp64, with no real consideration of making it workable with fp32.
7. Some methods have hard coded epsilons (1e-8) that are only suitable for fp64. (A reflection on 6).
8. With fp32 some methods report success when in fact they've done nothing, e.g. `minimize(rosen, np.array([10., 10.], np.float32), method='BFGS')`, or with 'L-BFGS-B', because of a variety of the reasons outlined here.
9. The internals of the methods need going over to see whether they're fp32 compatible.

If anyone has the appetite, they can take any C code in optimize and perform some regexes to;

- copy/replace `double`->`float`.
- change `fabs`->`fabsf`, `sqrt`->`sqrtf`, `pow`->`powf` etc... 
- change the BLAS/LAPACK calls to `dgemv`->`sgemv`, ...  (the complete list is in a separate header file)
- change the tol values

LLMs should be able to handle this much. Then the code can be tested against some tough problems. Longest file is 4000 lines so it's not really much (admittedly, my concept of a long file changed drastically in the last year). 

There is a renewed tendency to believe that "lower bitwidth saves space and gives performance" mainly due to ML folks but that is in general not true for these type of algorithms. It is true for many straightforward functions, say, softmaxing etc. But in the optimization algorithms the problem manifold does not get smoother when expressed in float32. So even if the function is convex the path you need to take to get to the minimum might require a few higher precision steps to breakout from a bottleneck or to dive into a "narrow well". It's very much like using a sharpie to write cursive and expecting legibility though tip of the sharpie is doing exactly the same motion as before.

I don't have much hope for success since current problems in the wild typically work with large gradients coming from ML problems hence overflow easily, but what do I know, maybe it works.
